sections.body: Course design and teaching is the work of turning a subject into a sequence of learning, then checking whether students actually learned it. Artificial intelligence is now used across that whole chain, from drafting learning outcomes and mapping them to weeks, to writing quiz items and problem sets, to building tutors that answer questions about one specific course. The common thread is that these systems work from a body of material a teacher already has, such as a syllabus, lecture notes, past exams or a textbook, and produce drafts that a person then edits. In practice this means faster first drafts of assessments, feedback that reaches students between classes, and early flags when someone stops submitting work. None of it replaces the judgement of the person who knows the students and the subject.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The parts that work reliably are the mechanical ones: generating variants of practice questions, aligning outcomes to topics, summarising notes into outlines, and answering factual questions grounded in supplied course material. The parts that remain hard are grading open-ended work fairly, judging whether a generated question actually tests the intended skill, and knowing when a struggling student needs a human rather than a nudge. Systems trained on general text carry assumptions that do not match a particular syllabus, so grounding in the course's own documents matters more than model size. Early warning tools raise real concerns about false positives and about labelling students, and their predictions are only as good as the data feeding them. Personalisation also tends to narrow what a student sees, which can quietly reduce exposure to material they did not know to ask for. The honest position is that these tools assist design and feedback, and the teacher still owns the standard.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages here follow the arc of building and running a course. Curriculum and Learning Outcomes is the starting point, covering how a subject is broken into outcomes and sequenced, which everything else depends on. Generating Assessments takes those outcomes and deals with producing questions, tasks and rubrics that match them. Personalised Learning and Early Warning sits on the student side, covering adaptive paths and the signals that suggest someone is falling behind. Course-Specific AI Tutors covers systems built around one course's own materials, which is where grounding and accuracy questions concentrate. Lecture Materials from Notes closes the loop, covering the conversion of raw notes into slides, handouts and explanations. A reader designing a course would start at the first, a reader teaching one would move between the middle three, and a reader preparing materials would go to the last.
